I checked the key against the stem. The dissolution is exothermic, so the temperature rises and ΔH = -q/n. Under-recording the salt (option B) shrinks n and raises |ΔH|, while over-recording it (option C, 5.50 g recorded, 5.00 g dissolved) inflates n and lowers |ΔH|, so C is correct.

Options A and D both raise q, so |ΔH| is too high. Each of A, B and D is wrong for a different reason.

One caveat is the effect of recording a larger salt mass on q. Calorimeter water mass is typically taken as the solution mass, which may include the salt mass. The stem doesn't say, so if the solution mass were taken as water plus salt, a larger recorded salt mass would also raise q slightly. The net effect would still be a lower |ΔH|, because n increases proportionally more than the solution mass. For 5.5 g versus 5.0 g, n rises by 10%. The mass in q rises by only 0.5 g out of about 105 g, which is under 0.5%. So C is still uniquely correct.

Option D, however, depends on the assumption that q is computed from the recorded water mass. That is standard. In option A, ΔT might be read as too high at the final temperature, which makes ΔT larger for an exothermic process, so A also gives |ΔH| too high. This is consistent.

The item fits topic 6.4 and skill 2.E. It has four short parallel options and a manageable load, with no calculation needed.
